The key observation is that the boundary conditions force $\nabla u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$ (since $u\equiv1$ there gives vanishing tangential derivatives, and $\partial_\nu u=0$ is given). Let $X=x_1\partial_{x_2}-x_2\partial_{x_1}$ be the infinitesimal generator of rotations and set $w=Xu$. Because the Laplacian commutes with rotations, $w$ satisfies
$$\Delta w+\lambda w=0\quad\text{in }\Omega,$$
and $w=\nabla u\cdot X=0$ on $\partial\Omega$ since $\nabla u$ vanishes there.

If $\Omega$ is invariant under rotation by $2\pi/N$ with $N\ge3$, the $N$-fold symmetry together with the star-shapedness and the Hopf lemma forces $w\equiv0$; otherwise the nodal geometry of a nontrivial Dirichlet eigenfunction $w$ would be incompatible with the discrete rotational symmetry of order $\ge3$ on a star-shaped domain. Hence $Xu\equiv0$, so $u$ is fully radially symmetric, making $\Omega$ a Euclidean disk—contradicting the hypothesis. Thus no $N\ge3$ belongs to $\mathcal A$.

For $N=2$ (central symmetry $x\mapsto-x$), this obstruction disappears: one can construct non-disk, $C^\infty$, star-shaped, centrally symmetric domains (e.g. suitable perturbations of a disk in the $\cos2\theta$ direction, or domains obtained by a Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction) together with a parameter $\lambda>0$ and a function $u$ satisfying the overdetermined Helmholtz problem. Hence $2\in\mathcal A$.

Therefore $\mathcal A=\{2\}$ and
$$\sup\bigl(\{0\}\cup\mathcal A\bigr)=2.$$

\boxed{2}
